text: Security and usability aren't a dial you can just turn toward 'more secure' and reliably get a safer instance. When legitimate access to data a user genuinely needs is too slow, too restricted, or too cumbersome to get through the proper channel, people don't simply stop doing their jobs. They find another way to get the work done — and that other way is almost always less secure than the control it replaced.

Shared credentials: if getting individual, properly scoped access takes a multi-week approval chain, a team under real deadline pressure will share one login among several people rather than wait it out. That one shared login now has no individual accountability at all — you've lost the entire audit trail, which is a strictly worse outcome than the over-broad role you were originally trying to avoid granting.

Shadow exports: if an analyst's field-level ACLs are so restrictive they can't assemble the view of data they actually need inside the platform, they export whatever they can see to a personal spreadsheet and keep building their own copy entirely outside ServiceNow. That spreadsheet has no ACLs, no audit log, no encryption, and probably lives in a personal folder nobody on the security team has ever looked at.

Shadow IT: if an entire workflow is too locked down to be usable at the team level, the team usually doesn't bother requesting a formal exception — they just stand up their own tool outside the governed environment entirely, whether that's a free SaaS app or a shared tracker. Now sensitive organizational data lives in a system with none of the controls the architect spent the previous lesson carefully designing.

The real architectural judgment isn't applying the strictest possible control uniformly across the whole instance — it's identifying exactly where the risk genuinely justifies friction, like approval-chain overrides or regulated financial and health data, and making access to everything else as close to frictionless as that actual risk tolerates. Uniform maximum restriction looks impressive on an audit checklist and performs badly in practice, because it manufactures the very workarounds that defeat it.

Watch for the early warning signals before they harden into shadow IT: unusual spikes in exports from sensitive tables, helpdesk tickets asking for someone else's login, or a department quietly running its own tracker that duplicates data already sitting in ServiceNow. Each one means the fix is redesigning the access itself, not issuing a reminder about policy compliance. Next, a full worked lab applying exactly that judgment to a real finance team's expense data.
